extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners and USPTO disciplinary officials (OED), administrative law judges, and attorneys practicing before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures governing disciplinary proceedings against practitioners before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (OED complaints, interim suspension, default, findings of misconduct, and sanctions). Focuses on criminal convictions (e.g., manslaughter) and their effect on fitness to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of complaint (PTO Rule 11.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint may be served on a respondent 'By mailing a copy of the complaint by "Express Mail;" first-class mail, or any delivery service that provides ability to confirm delivery or attempted delivery.' A respondent who is a registered practitioner is to be served at the address provided to OED pursuant to § 11.11.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mailing to the practitioner's last address known to OED (including to an institutional/prison address) suffices; return-receipt/other delivery confirmation evidence can demonstrate adequate service. The Decision found adequate service based on mailing and prison receipt documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time for answer (PTO Rule 11.36(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: An answer to a complaint shall be filed within the time set in the complaint but in no event shall that time be less than thirty days from the date the complaint is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complaint/Final Order here notified Respondent of a 30-day deadline; the tribunal noted minor discrepancies about the 30-day start date but found them immaterial in context. Practitioners must file a written answer within the required period to avoid default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default judgment consequences (PTO Rule 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default causes the respondent to be 'deemed to have admitted all of the allegations in the Complaint.' Default also prevents development of a record regarding mitigating circumstances and supports entry of sanctions based on admitted facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim suspension/exclusion for conviction of serious crime (37 C.F.R. § 11.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.25 allows for the expeditious interim suspension (exclusion) of a practitioner convicted of a serious crime; the Director may issue a Final Order under § 11.25(b) excluding the practitioner from practice on an interim basis and refer the Complaint for disciplinary proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director served a Notice and Order and, after a practitioner failed to timely respond, entered a Final Order excluding him under § 11.25(b). Practitioners convicted of serious crimes may be temporarily excluded pending formal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A criminal conviction (e.g., manslaughter) may be found to constitute 'disreputable or gross misconduct' under this subsection when the conduct shocks the moral sense of the community or otherwise demonstrates unfitness to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on illegal conduct involving moral turpitude (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not engage in illegal conduct involving moral turpitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conviction of a crime involving moral turpitude is explicitly included (see § 10.23(c)(1)) and supports a finding under (b)(3). The Decision found voluntary manslaughter to be a crime involving moral turpitude and thus a violation of (b)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not 'engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'other' requires that conduct charged under (b)(6) be distinct from conduct charged under subsections (b)(1)-(5). The tribunal held that the same facts cannot support both (b)(3) and (b)(6); if facts support (b)(3), (b)(6) based on the same facts must be dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conviction as illustrative conduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct which constitutes a violation of paragraphs (a) and (b) includes, but is not limited to: (1) Conviction of a criminal offense involving moral turpitude, dishonesty or breach of trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision applied § 10.23(c)(1) to hold that a first-degree manslaughter conviction is a conviction 'involving moral turpitude' and therefore violates §§ 10.23(a) and (b)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and judicial interpretation of 'moral turpitude'
rubrics_metrics.description: Black's Law Dictionary: 'conduct that is contrary to justice, honesty or morality.' Case law: moral turpitude generally means 'shameful wickedness' or acts 'contrary to the accepted and customary rule of right and duty between people.' Voluntary manslaughter has been held to involve moral turpitude in multiple jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision cites case law (e.g., Harris v. Dean, Franklin, Frnniclin, and others) and Black's to support treating voluntary manslaughter as moral turpitude. Practitioners facing convictions should note these authoritative definitions and precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of discipline available (PTO Rule 11.20(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The following types of discipline may be imposed upon a practitioner: (1) Exclusion from practice before the Office; (2) Suspension from practice before the Office for an appropriate period of time; (3) Reprimand or censure; (4) Probation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office may select among these sanctions based on the nature of violations and the § 11.54(b) factors (duty violated; intent; injury; aggravating/mitigating factors). OED requested exclusion in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to be considered in determining penalty (PTO Rule 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining any penalty the following four factors 'must be considered if they are applicable:' (1) Whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tribunal applied these factors and found (based on the admitted facts) violation of duty to society, intentional/knowing action, and a death resulting, supporting the sanction of exclusion. The lack of a developed record (due to default) limited inquiry into mitigating circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations supporting exclusion (violent crime, death, moral turpitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conviction for crimes involving moral turpitude, violent crimes, or crimes causing death are cited as grounds supporting exclusion/disbarment from practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision and cited authorities (cases involving attorneys convicted of violent crimes, manslaughter, vehicular homicide, firearm offenses) emphasize protecting the public and profession. Precedents include cases where disbarment/exclusion was imposed despite mitigating factors; courts emphasize gravity of misconduct and risk to clients/public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that 'other' conduct be distinct for § 10.23(b)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: To give the word 'other' significance in § 10.23(b)(6), the facts alleged to constitute a violation of subsection (b)(6) must be other than facts alleged to constitute violations of another provision of § 10.23(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision follows USPTO appellate tribunal precedent (In re Cole) to dismiss Count 3 (b)(6) where the same facts supported (b)(3); charging the same facts under both subsections is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal and post-exclusion procedures (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.55, 11.58, 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals from an initial decision must be filed with the Director of OED pursuant to § 11.55 within 30 days and must include exceptions and supporting reasons. § 11.58 addresses responsibilities in case of exclusion; § 11.60 concerns petition for reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file a timely appeal is deemed acceptance of the decision and waiver of further administrative and judicial review. The Decision directs respondent to these sections for procedural options following exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedent and external disciplinary standards in sanctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining appropriate discipline, OED and the tribunal may rely on external authorities (state bar disciplinary decisions, ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions) and prior cases addressing similar misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Decision cites state disciplinary cases and ABA Standards (e.g., ABA Standards §5.11(a)) to justify exclusion for intentional killing or violent crimes, showing that disciplinary reasoning and sanctions may be informed by analogous authorities.
